title: Filtering with WHERE
subtitle: AND, OR, NOT, IN, BETWEEN, LIKE, and NULL
author: KERNAL Team

whyItExists.problem: SELECT * FROM table returns millions of rows. You need to filter down to only the rows that match specific conditions.
whyItExists.solution: The WHERE clause filters rows before returning them. Combine conditions with AND, OR, NOT. Use BETWEEN for ranges, IN for value lists, LIKE for pattern matching, IS NULL for missing data.
whyItExists.whenToUse: Anytime you want a subset of rows — users from a city, orders above a price, products matching a search term.
whyItExists.whenNotToUse: To filter grouped results (after GROUP BY), use HAVING — not WHERE. WHERE runs before aggregation.

explainModes.beginner: WHERE is like a filter. SELECT * FROM users WHERE city = 'Delhi' returns only users from Delhi. Add AND to require multiple conditions, OR to allow either. LIKE with % matches any text.
explainModes.simple: WHERE condition. Operators: =, !=, <, >, <=, >=. AND, OR, NOT with parentheses for grouping. IN (val1, val2, val3) — match any. BETWEEN a AND b — inclusive range. LIKE 'pattern' — % for any chars, _ for one char. IS NULL / IS NOT NULL — test for missing values. Never use = NULL (always IS NULL).
explainModes.standard: Condition evaluation uses three-valued logic (TRUE, FALSE, NULL). Any comparison with NULL returns NULL (not FALSE) — which is why = NULL never works. Short-circuit evaluation: A AND B stops at A if A is FALSE. For case-insensitive LIKE in SQLite use LIKE (it's case-insensitive by default for ASCII). In PostgreSQL, ILIKE for case-insensitive. IN with subquery: WHERE id IN (SELECT user_id FROM orders).
explainModes.technical: Predicate pushdown: the engine evaluates WHERE early to reduce the row set before other operations. Index usage: = and range (<, >, BETWEEN) on indexed columns use index scans. LIKE 'prefix%' can use an index; LIKE '%suffix' cannot (full scan). NOT IN with NULLs is a classic bug: NOT IN (1, 2, NULL) returns no rows because NULL comparisons return NULL. Use NOT EXISTS instead.
explainModes.deepDive: SQL's three-valued logic (Codd, 1979) exists because NULL represents 'unknown.' NULL AND TRUE = NULL, NULL OR TRUE = TRUE, NULL AND FALSE = FALSE. Practical implications: rows where a condition evaluates to NULL are excluded (same as FALSE). Coalesce(col, default) converts NULL to a value. IS DISTINCT FROM / IS NOT DISTINCT FROM treat NULL as a normal value (NULLs are equal to each other).

questions.question: Why does WHERE price = NULL return no rows, even if some prices are NULL?
options: NULL is a reserved keyword and can't be compared
Because = NULL evaluates to NULL (unknown), not TRUE — use IS NULL instead
You need to quote it: WHERE price = 'NULL'
questions.explanation: SQL uses three-valued logic. NULL represents 'unknown.' Any comparison with NULL (=, !=, <, >) returns NULL, not TRUE or FALSE. Rows where the condition evaluates to NULL are excluded. Use IS NULL and IS NOT NULL to test for missing values.

faq.q: What is the difference between IN and = with OR?
faq.a: WHERE city IN ('Delhi', 'Mumbai') is exactly equivalent to WHERE city = 'Delhi' OR city = 'Mumbai' — just shorter and more readable. IN is preferred for 3+ values. IN also accepts a subquery: WHERE id IN (SELECT user_id FROM orders).

In SQLite: LIKE is case-insensitive for ASCII characters (A matches a). In PostgreSQL: LIKE is case-sensitive; use ILIKE for case-insensitive. In MySQL: case-sensitivity depends on the collation. Best practice: normalise your data (store lowercase emails) to avoid depending on case-insensitive matching.

examples: WHERE status = 'active' AND created_at > '2024-01-01' — filter recent active users
WHERE email LIKE '%@gmail.com' — find users with Gmail addresses
WHERE deleted_at IS NULL — soft-delete pattern (only fetch non-deleted rows)
